title: Carbonara
subtitle: Roman pasta with eggs, guanciale, and pecorino
excerpt: The Roman pasta that requires no cream: spaghetti tossed with a silky sauce made from egg yolks, guanciale, and pecorino, kept fluid by the residual heat of the pasta and a little starchy cooking water. Done in under 20 minutes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Carbonara is one of the four canonical pastas of Roman cuisine, alongside cacio e pepe, amatriciana, and gricia. The dish is relatively recent in origin: the earliest documented recipes date from the 1950s, and its exact history is contested, with theories ranging from wartime American influence (bacon and eggs) to derivation from the older gricia. The defining elements are guanciale (cured pig's cheek), eggs (whole eggs and/or yolks), pecorino romano, and black pepper. Pancetta is the accepted substitute for guanciale outside Italy; bacon is a last resort. Cream is never added in the traditional Roman preparation: it was invented to prevent the eggs from scrambling, but the authentic technique achieves this without cream by removing the pan from heat before adding the egg mixture and working quickly. The carbonara wars — cream or no cream — represent a genuine divide between Italian tradition and widespread international adaptation.

content.text: The pan must be off the heat when the egg mixture goes in. A hot pan will scramble the eggs. Work fast: add the egg mixture to the hot pasta, toss continuously, and add splashes of pasta water to keep the sauce fluid and glossy. The residual heat from the pasta and pan is exactly enough to cook the eggs to a creamy consistency. If the eggs start to set into curds, add more pasta water immediately.

items.preparation: cut into 1 cm cubes or lardons; or guanciale
finely grated; use pecorino romano if available

content.text: Whisk together the eggs, extra yolk, grated cheese, and black pepper in a bowl. Set aside. Cook the pancetta or guanciale in a large pan over medium heat until the fat has rendered and the pieces are golden at the edges. Remove from the heat.
Cook the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Reserve 200 ml of pasta cooking water before draining. Drain the pasta.

Add the hot pasta to the pan with the pancetta. Remove the pan entirely from the heat. Pour the egg mixture over the pasta and toss continuously, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is thick, glossy, and clings to every strand. The whole process should take about 1 minute. Serve immediately with extra cheese and pepper.
